dataset.name: Litter Production and Foliar Nutrient Resorption in Pioneer and Non-Pioneer Species in a Selective Logging Experiment in the Central Amazon, BIONTE, ZF-2, Manaus, 2022-23
description: This dataset was collected near the city of Manaus, Brazil, at the Experimental Station of Tropical Forestry (EEST, aka “ZF2”), inside the BIONTE (BIOmass and NuTrient Experiment). The experiment included three levels of increasing selective logging intensity, along with control, with 1-hectare permanent plots (12 total) located at the center of 4-hectare treatment plots. The vegetation has a high floristic diversity, the soils of the region are poor in nutrients, and the topography is characterized by plateaus (where BIONTE is located), and also valley bottoms and slopes. Three treatments of differing logging intensities were applied in the BIONTE experiment (T1, T2 and T3). The study was conducted in Treatment 3 (Block I – permanent plot), which represents the most intensive logging treatment, with 69% of the basal area (m²∙ha⁻¹) removed in 1988. The present dataset spans the period from May 1, 2022, to May 1, 2023. The data package includes leaf_nutrient_data, litterfall_total_data, leaf_litterfall_species_specific_data, and species_info, all provided in .csv format. These formats allow users to process and analyze the data in various software applications and programming languages, such as Python and R. This dataset was collected to advance knowledge on nutrient cycling in Amazonian forests, specifically distinguishing between species with two distinct functional traits: fast-growing and slow-growing. It also aims to improve Earth System Models, such as the E3SM Functionally Assembled Terrestrial Ecosystem Simulator (FATES). Additionally, it was used in a paper currently in preparation (Carvalho et al., in prep.), which aims to quantify seasonal litter production and foliar nutrient resorption in pioneer (fast-growing) and non-pioneer (slow-growing) tree species in the central Amazon. Specifically, it seeks to answer two key questions: 1) Is there a difference in leaf litter production, leaf nutrient flux and leaf nutrient concentration between pioneers and non-pioneers species? Is there a difference in the efficiency of foliar nutrient resorption between pioneers and non-pioneers species?

measurementTechnique:
Plant material (green leaves and litter)
This dataset was collected near Manaus, Brazil, at ZF-2 site, inside the BIONTE project (Treatment 3 – Block I – permanent plot) from 20220501 to 20230501. Measurements were made on pioneer and non-pioneer tree species in upland high-clay content soils of plateaus. We selected six tree species (three pioneers and three non-pioneers) with three replicates for each species, resulting in a total of eighteen (18) monitored individuals (Species_Info.csv). We quantified the seasonal production of species-specific leaf litter using deposition collectors and assessed the retranslocation of foliar nutrients by analyzing species-specific samples of fresh (green) and senescent (litter) leaves. These samples were evaluated for nutrient content and nutrient retranslocation efficiency.

Phenology
Bi-weekly phenological monitoring of the trees was conducted to determine their phenological patterns and to relate with species-specific litter deposition. For a clear view of the canopies and, more precisely, the branches of individual trees, an 8x21mm binocular was used to detail all the occurring phenological stages in the studied individuals. All observations of phenophases were recorded on a field sheet containing specific information regarding flowering (floral buds, flowering start, flowering peak/middle, flowering end), fruiting (green fruits, fruit abortion, ripe fruits, fruit/seed dissemination), and leaf flushing (new leaves), as recommended by Fournier and Charpantier (1975).

Litterfall Quantification
Four litter deposition collectors were installed and systematically distributed within the crown for each individual tree (72 collectors in total). Species-specific leaf litter and other litter fractions were collected biweekly from May 2022 to April 2023 to prevent material decomposition within the collectors. Each collector was constructed with a square structure covering 0.25 m2, resulting in a total sample area of 1 m2 per tree. The collectors were made from plastic pipes and included a central basket constructed with a 1 mm mesh nylon screen, positioned 1 m above ground level.
A composite sample of total litterfall production was obtained from the four collectors installed around each tree. The bi-weekly collections from the collectors (composite sample) for each tree were combined into monthly samples. Monthly total environmental litterfall production and species-specific leaf litter production was obtained by summing the bi-weekly collections per tree. Total environmental litterfall production was expressed in Mg ha-1 year-1 to allow for comparison with other studies. The monthly composite samples were stored in zip-lock plastic bags to prevent moisture loss, and transported to the laboratory for sorting and processing within 24-48 hours.
To assist in the identification of leaves and other parts in the litter, herbarium specimens (exsiccates) were made from each target species. The litter from each composite sample was separated into two major fractions: species-specific leaf litter and “other parts”, which included fine branches (diameter ≤ 2 cm), reproductive material (flowers, fruits, and seeds), miscellaneous (unidentified plant/animal material), and non-identified leaf material (from other non-target species). This separation was necessary due to the difficulty in identifying the components of “other parts” fraction at the species level. Total environmental litterfall production was quantified by summing the species-specific leaf litter with other fractions.
All fractions inside each composite sample, including species-specific leaf litter and “other parts” (fine branches, reproductive material, non-specific leaf litter and miscellaneous) were separated and weighed. The fractions were dried in an oven for 48-60 hours at 60°C. After the drying period, the dried mass (in grams) was determined, and weighing was conducted daily until a constant weight was achieved. The scale used in this study was an analytical balance (TOLEDO model PS 360), and the oven was a TECNAL TE-394/3.

Chemical analyses
The samples of green leaves and species-specific leaf litter from the selected species were ground in a Wiley-type mill. To prevent cross-contamination, the mill was thoroughly cleaned after processing each sample. Following this, the ground samples were stored in Eppendorf tubes and sent to the Soil and Plant Tissue Analysis Laboratory (LASP) at EMBRAPA Western Amazon for chemical analysis of N, P, K, Ca, and Mg, conducted according to the methodology outlined by Malavolta, Vitti, and Oliveira (1997).
Hot acid digestion was performed for all elements. Nitro-perchloric extraction was used for P, K, Ca, and Mg, with the analytical determination of K, Ca, and Mg carried out by Atomic Absorption Spectrophotometry, and P determined using Optical Spectrophotometry. For N, sulfuric acid extraction was performed, and the analytical determination was conducted using a Kjeldahl distillation apparatus.

Species-specific Foliar Nutrient Resorption
The collection of branches containing green leaves was conducted monthly, selecting between 5 and 10 leaves per tree. Each set of samples were labeled and stored in a zip-lock plastic bag, taking care to maintain the integrity of the samples. When necessary, the samples were refrigerated until the material was sorted, within a 24-hour period after collection. Whenever possible, branches from each tree were collected that were in full sunlight, and when in the understory, branches were collected from the upper part of the canopy. In the laboratory, preferably mature leaves without signals of herbivory and good phytosanitary aspects, were selected. The green foliage was dried at 60°C for about until a constant weight was achieved (approximately 48 hours).
The resorption efficiency (NuRE) is the proportion of nutrients retranslocated before leaf abscission in relation to the ratio between the nutrient concentration in the senescent leaf and the concentration in the green leaf, as per the equation. The resorption efficiency can be calculated based on the average of representative tree individuals from each group (Killinbeck, 1996; Sun et al., 2023).
NuRE (%) = (Nugr - Nusen)/ Nugr ) × 100
Where Nugr represent the nutrient concentration of the green leaves, Nusen represent the nutrient concentration of senescent material, on a dry weight basis.
